system:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: To start small, which of the drone operating companies do you work for, and what is the very first thing you do when you log in each day?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Thinking about the last drone flight you dealt with, what was your involvement in it?

Q4

I can also call off a flight. However, I know nothing about software and accounts and passwords inside the service are not used since staff accounts are issued by the platform company outside it.
The question: How does a request for a flight first reach you, and who does it come from?

Q6
The answer just before it: I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, but our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. I can also call off a flight.
The question: How do you work out today which of your drones could get to where a job starts?

Q7
The answer just before it: I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. However, our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, and choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility.
The question: What details about a drone or a job do you need to see to tell if that drone can reach where the job starts?

Q8
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Before you sign off a flight to leave, what do you check by hand because you don't trust anyone or anything else to get it right?

Q9
The answer just before it: I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight, and it is my legal responsibility to choose the drone and the way it flies.
The question: What makes you decide to call off a flight?

Q10
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day on the job, and what made it so bad?

Q11
The answer just before it: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.
The question: When a drone restarts in flight or radio coverage drops out, what happens on your end, and what do you need to know right after it comes back?

Q12
The answer just before it: I worry about radio coverage being patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about reports from drones arriving late, out of order, more than once, or not at all through relay stations. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.
The question: When a closure comes into force while drones are already in the air, how do you find out about it, and what do you have to do right away?

Q13
The answer just before it: I worry that a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.
The question: When a sudden closure applies at once or an area is widened, how do you check if any of your drones are affected?

Q14
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You mentioned reports from drones arriving late, out of order, or more than once through relay stations—what problems does that cause for you when you are watching a flight?

Q15
The answer just before it: I worry because nobody watches every drone at every moment, and one person may be responsible for hundreds. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, causing reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.
The question: Since one person may be responsible for hundreds of drones and cannot watch every one at every moment, how do you know when something has gone wrong with one of them?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When a drone has an issue—like a battery draining faster than planned or an incident on a flight—what do you need to find out or look back at right afterward?

Q17
The answer just before it: I worry that batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. I do not know what I need to find out or look back at right afterward.
The question: How do you work with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk—what do they hand over to you, and what do you hand over to them?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What are you most afraid a new service would get wrong or do badly for your work?

Q19
The answer just before it: I worry about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather. I also worry that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.
The question: Thinking about your company's fleet, jobs, and sites compared to the other operating companies on the platform, what are your concerns or rules around who can see what?

Q20
The answer just before it: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We accept sharing airspace information because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
The question: Are there any other parts of your job, rules you must follow, or problems you deal with that we haven't talked about yet?

Q21
The answer just before it: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way before signing off a flight. I also follow the EU drone operation rules and the EU U-space rules. Furthermore, personal data of staff is covered by the GDPR.
The question: Under the EU drone operation and U-space rules, what records or proof of your sign-offs and decisions do you need to keep?
